newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Fear of shifting rubble hinders hunt for survivors.
newsitem.headline: Fear of shifting rubble hinders hunt for survivors.

text.p: Attempts to find more survivors beneath the rubble of a landslide at an Australian ski resort were frustrated on Sunday by fears of further slippages in rubble.
Police said work at the site of Wednesday's disaster was interrupted several times overnight as rubble continued to shift ominously.
One huge boulder moved several centimetres and one of the large concrete slabs under which more victims were believed to be entombed slipped just before sunrise.
"There has been some concern about the stability of the site," police spokesman Allan Small told Reuters. "The movement of some rocks and boulders has been giving some anxiety."
Rescuers, who miraculously plucked a survivor from a concrete tomb beneath the rubble on Saturday, located another two bodies during the night work, bringing the death toll to eight.
So far, only four bodies have been removed from the mangled heap of concrete, twisted metal, dirt and splintered trees at Thredbo, southwest of Sydney.
Police said Stuart Diver, 27, the only survivor so far of the landslide which destroyed two ski lodges late on Wednesday night, was in serious but stable condition in a hospital in nearby Canberra.
Work would continue at the wreckage site on Sunday with most of the workers concentrating on shoring up unstable chunks of rubble.
The four bodies still trapped should be removed on Sunday morning, police said. They declined to identify the dead. Still missing in the debris was Diver's wife, Sally.
She was with him in bed on Wednesday night when the slide tore through the resort, sending one lodge crashing into another below.
Canberra Hospital's emergency specialist, Dr Bob Dunn, said Diver, a ski instructor, might need surgery for frostbite.

Diver, described by friends and police as a survival expert and fitness fanatic, spent about 64 hours sandwiched between thick wedges of concrete in a cramped air pocket 10 metres (33 feet) beneath the surface for three freezing nights.
He was expected to remain in hospital for at least a few days for "extensive treatment", Dunn said.
Diver was found after a fireman heard a muffled voice but rescuers, digging by hand so as not to dislodge the concrete slabs, took 12 hours to free him.
"A miracle has occurred ...," police chief superintendent Charlie Sanderson said after Diver's calls were heard under the tonnes of rubble just before dawn on Saturday.
More than 150 friends and onlookers cheered as Diver was lifted out of a small hole in the rubble just before sunset on Saturday.
He was placed on a stretcher and quickly covered with several blankets, including a silver thermal blanket, before being carried up a steep slope to a waiting ambulance.
He was later flown by helicopter to a hospital in Canberra, about 150 km (90 miles) north of Thredbo, while bells rang out from the village's little chapel.
Borne on a stretcher and wearing a heavy neck-brace, Diver won more cheers on arrival in Canberra, where a crowd of about 60 people shouted their best wishes and tooted car horns.

Diver was caught between concrete slabs which saved him from being crushed and created an air pocket that insulated him from the freezing overnight temperatures of minus 12 degrees Celsius (about 10 degrees Fahrenheit).
Just before dawn on Saturday fireman Steve Hirst, who was clearing concrete while suspended by a rope, heard a noise and called for silence on the mountain.
"I yelled out: 'rescue team working overhead, can anyone hear me'," Hirst said. "I repeated the call and had a voice come strongly back to me."
"A gentleman identified himself and said he was in fine spirits and doing quite well and uninjured, just extremely cold," he said. Diver's first words were: 'I can hear you'."
Diver was lying on his back, with only 30 cm (12 inches) to move his head and 40 to 50 cm (15 to 19 inches) to shift his feet.
There was a cold stream of water running down his side.
Rescuers managed to feed Diver a liquid nutrient solution and warm air was pumped under his jumper to help raise his body temperature while rescuers kept digging to free him.
